utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. After the untimely resignment of Judge Szenasi, the President of this Tribunal assigned Judge Mumba as a Judge in this proceedings. Judge Mumba began her function last Monday and she will not be able to attend this hearing, so in accordance with the Rule 15 bis, the remaining Judges decided to continue our proceedings. This hearing is in accordance with the decision on the parties' request regarding the deposition evidence of one witness rendered by this Trial Chamber on the 12th of May, 2005. In general, the Trial Chamber is reluctant to grant the recalling of a witness who has provided testimony by way of deposition for the reason that a party has failed to ask questions which may prove important to its case. However, the Trial Chamber believes the witness is an individual mentioned in the allegation of paragraph 10 of the indictment and as such could have specific unique knowledge as to that particular allegation in the indictment and his evidence in this respect may prove to be pivotal evidence in this case. So we decided to ask him some questions. The purpose of questioning by the Judges will be limited to the allegation in the paragraph 10 of the indictment, and after that both parties may raise some questions, but also in the scope of the paragraph 10 of the indictment. Well, could we connect with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We have some technical problem. Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Very well, in fact, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Mr. Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we have the questions, I would like to remind you the Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. It's been indicated to me that the accused, Mr. Halilovic, cannot hear anything at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In particular, he's unable to hear Mr. Karic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I have been advised that there's some technical problem at this stage, so we have to take a break for about 10 minutes, and we'll resume at 20 past 9.00. --- Break taken at 9.09 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I believe that I have to apologise to you for the delay. Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand? No?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hear the interpreter, but I do not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Maybe there's some problem with the channel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try it again, to see whether you could hear him or not. If not, please let us know as soon as possible. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, at the very beginning I have to remind you the Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, that you have the right to object to making a statement which may tend to incriminate yourself. But that Trial Chamber may, however, compel you to answer the question. That testimony so compelled shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against you for any offence other than the forced testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour, I understand completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, could you please tell us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: My name is Vehbija Karic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And when do you think you were born?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 21st of April, 1938 in Podgrad, municipality of Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And were you in the Yugoslavia People's Army at the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army. I was an officer. I was a colonel by rank in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And when did you join the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the ABiH on the 8th of April, 1992, after I left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And when did you --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: On that day I joined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And when did you retire from the army?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I retired in late May 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And with what rank?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: With the rank of army brigadier of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. During which time have you been in Grabovica? Could you give us the date of arrival and departure, if possible.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: This was at the beginning of September. I will look up the exact date in my diary. In early September 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And what's the departure time? Or how long did you stay in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: How long did I stay in Grabovica? I was there less than an hour with a group of people who looked around the -- we were there on two occasions expecting the arrival of the units from Sarajevo. We decided to accommodate those billets because Jablanica was overbooked by refugees from Prozor and that part of Herzegovina. We had problems with accommodation, so we decided that some of those units should be billeted in Grabovica. Rifat Bilajac was with me at the time, as well as Zicro Suljevic, Namik, and we went around to see the inhabitants of the village, asked them whether they had enough space in their houses to receive a number of soldiers for a brief period of several days. They told us that there was no problem, that they would accommodate them in one room. These were usually elderly people, husbands and wives. There were also some younger people from Konjic who had come to be with their relatives, but mostly all of them agreed. After that, the units were billeted there. After 24 hours, after one night spent in Grabovica by those units, we came to see them the next day to see if there were any problems, and so on and so forth. So I was there on two occasions with a group of people from the inspection team when we went to review the situation regarding their accommodation, the accommodation of the units. I think that this was on the 7th or the 8th of September, this second time, after one night in Grabovica, after they had spent one night in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. In your answer, you said that "So we decided that some of those units should be billeted in Grabovica." Would you please be more specific to tell us who are "we." Are they members of the inspection team?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, members of the inspection team. Rifat Bilajac, Zicro Suljevic, I myself, and Namik Dzankovic went to see if it was possible to billet the troops there the day before, and then after spending one night there - I think that this was on the 8th in the morning, on the 8th of September -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And how about --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: -- when we visited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry. How about Mr. Halilovic? Did he go there with you?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic? No, he didn't. He wasn't in Jablanica at the time. He was somewhere out in the field. And we did that without his physical presence, which was normal and in keeping with the idea of billeting the troops for the forthcoming operation, when we were coordinating the combat activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you meet -- did Mr. Halilovic involved in the decision of billeting the soldiers in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I think that he found out about it indirectly and that objective was to billet the people so that they could rest after arriving from Sarajevo following a march, which was quite tiring. These people needed to be accommodated. And in general, the area in Jablanica was overbooked with refugees and we didn't have much logistics resources. We didn't have accommodation in tents or bivouacs. As far as the measures that some other army might have taken which would not be in such dire circumstances as we were concerning materiel and logistics, in order to accommodate troops outside of inhabited areas, we had to do it this way. Before that, we got the consent of the inhabitants that there would be no problems and that they agreed to billet the people. To this very day I am not sure whether Sefer Halilovic knew or not about this minor detail, but we were the ones who were actually considering this problem. Those days he was absent, he was touring, he was in Sarajevo, Konjic, and in other places in the area of preparation of troops for the forthcoming operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And during your stay in Grabovica, in your testimony you told us that you stayed one night there. And where did you stay that night in the village?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that we spent the night there but that the troops were billeted on the night of the 7th and the 8th in the village of Grabovica. These were units of the 9th Mountain Brigade and a part of the 10th Mountain Brigade as well as a smaller group from Solakovic's battalion. We billeted them there. We were there in conversation the day before the troops were going to arrive. I think that this was on the 7th. Before the troops arrived, we talked with the inhabitants of Grabovica and reached an agreement with them that they had nothing against receiving this number of soldiers to spend the night there, and then we returned to Jablanica, where we continued with our activities. The next day, on the 8th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: -- we as a group went to visit. We as a group went to visit Grabovica. We were driven by Huso Alic. Rifat Bilajac, Zicro Suljevic, I was there, my son with there as an escort, and Namik Dzankovic as security officer were in this group. This was the inspection team. We stayed with the inhabitants and we were in conversation with them, the ones who had received soldiers to stay the night with them, and we asked the soldiers if they had rested well, how they felt, if there were any problems. After an hour, in our view there were no problems. The soldiers were received well. They were in a good mood. They had slept well after a tiring march to reach that place. Some of them were actually fishing. Some had lit a fire and they were barbecuing something around those fires. In any case, the mood was as if it was a picnic. There were no problems at all. And after about an hour, we returned to Jablanica to continue with our further activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. In your testimony, you said that "There were units of the 9th Mountain Brigade." Is it 9th Mountain Brigade or 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: The 9th Mountain Brigade, commanded by Celo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you -- in your testimony, you also said that you had an opportunity to talk to the soldiers, if they had rested well. Do you know who are those soldiers and which units they were from?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: It is hard for me to answer if I know which soldiers they were because when we saw them, they happened to be in the yard in front of the house where they happened to be, and we would stop as our group -- as a group, this group that was in the vehicle. We would stop and for a moment we would ask them if they had a rest, if they slept well, if there were any problems, was everything all right. Everything was all right. And then we went on from house to house, so that then we actually went to the yards of all the inhabitants asking if there were any problems. There were none. I don't know if these were only soldiers of the 9th Brigade or the 10th Brigade - I can't really say, but both were in that particular area - who came up to us or whom we approached and had this contact with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you see or meet Mr. Halilovic during your stay in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: No. No. Halilovic wasn't with us in Grabovica, not when we went to see if it would be possible to billet the troops there or afterwards. He wasn't in Jablanica during that particular period, those few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now I will pass the questions to Judge El Mahdi and Judge El Mahdi will continue to ask you some questions. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to ask a few questions from you concerning your deposition. You said that Mr. Halilovic - I quote you -- [In English] "found about it indirectly." [Interpretation] And you speak of the question of the troops being billeted with civilians. So could you explain your answer, if you please. What do you actually mean when you say he was indirectly made aware?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: As part of our previous contacts with Halilovic, I remember that, amongst other things, we talked about the question of billeting the units coming from the area of Sarajevo. Those people needed to be accommodated so that they could rest. I cannot say. I'm not sure if it was said in his presence at the time that these people would be billeted in the village of Grabovica because a number of the fighters we accommodated in Gornja Jablanica in some prefabricated houses or huts, also with the civilian population, and there were no problems at all. And specifically when the crime happened on the 9th -- of the 8th to the 9th of December, when we informed Halilovic about it the next day, on the 10th, even though Namik Dzankovic told him about it in Jablanica once he returned from the field on the 9th in the evening, it's possible that he understood then that a part of the 9th and 10th Brigade units and those of the Independent Battalion were billeted in the village of Grabovica. We thought that this was normal. The people needed to be accommodated. This was not something that was done by force, forcibly billeting these people into somebody's -- in somebody's apartments. We asked the people if they wanted to receive them. The houses were usually larger, occupied by one or two elderly people as a rule. There were also barns. There were other farm buildings. And there was no problem facing us. We asked them properly would it be possible to accommodate these people, and they all agreed to that, without a problem. So I personally think that Sefer found out about this event specifically, that the units were billeted in Grabovica, only after learning about an information about the crime that occurred in the night between the 8th and the 9th of September. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll put to you another question: This question of billeting of the troops, was that within the purview of the inspection team?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Once we left Sarajevo, when we received our assignment to coordinate combat operations and some other activities relating to the subordination of the commands of the 4th, 3rd, and 6th Corps, felt it was normal, since we were out in the field anyway and we were given these assignments, that it was normal also to deal with the billeting issue of the people who were going to be placed at our disposal. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] What was the role of the leader or chief of this inspection team? Were you responsible for taking decisions without his agreement, without his consent?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, the authority to coordinate combat operations and do our job regarding coordination in the Neretva 93 operation from the point of view taken at the time, which was before the crime occurred and before the units did what they did against those civilians who had put them up in their own homes and gave them an opportunity to rest, it would have been logical to expect that nothing like that would happen, particularly not with people who had arrived from Sarajevo. The syndrome that prevailed in Herzegovina among the fighters - because this had been preceded by a series of clashes between the HVO and our army - did not apply in Sarajevo. In Sarajevo there was still an atmosphere of unity between us and the HVO. Even less could we have expected to see this done by troops who had been brought in from Sarajevo. They were not encumbered with the deteriorating relations in Herzegovina as it were, and this was definitely not something that we could expect. Even as we speak, I still believe it was perfectly natural for us to find accommodation for those people, since we were the inspection team in charge of coordination. This was an issue that -- that it was down to us to deal with. We weren't only meant to coordinate combat operations but also to create the prerequisites in order to have any sort of coordination at all, to bring the units there and to get them ready for any upcoming combat operations. Even as we speak, I still believe that was the natural thing to do. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But it was another question I was asking from you. My question related to the responsibilities, the competencies of the inspection team and the duties and competencies of the chief of this inspection team. And a decision, if it belongs to the competence of this team, was it logical or did it conform to military necessities if it was taken without the approval or without the knowledge of the leader of the team? That is, you took this decision by yourself without putting him on notice, without letting him know?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we, as an inspection team, believed at the time that it was perfectly logical that a number of tasks, given our experience and our knowledge as long-serving officers in a more general context were to be assumed by us and that there was no need to go and look for Sefer, who wasn't present when the units arrived. We needed to put them up, and the general idea was to find accommodation for the units, to give them an opportunity to rest so that they could be ready for the upcoming combat operations. We did not see this as an act of insubordination, and this was certainly no slight to his position as the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, another question: Were you aware of any complaint during your stay or passage in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: You mean as a group as we were touring the area? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] No, when you were in town, when you were going through Grabovica, when you were in Grabovica. Because if I understand you well, you went twice to Grabovica, on two occasions. So for the moment I'm talking about the second time. Was there no complaint made by the citizens or by the troops concerning the behaviours or the relationship between the troops and the citizens of the city?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were no complaints or negative connotations. It was a run-of-the-mill situation where we asked the soldiers whether they'd had a good rest, and the same applied to the locals. There was no friction, no negative atmosphere. There was nothing for us to be concerned about. We would go from house to house. We would meet a group of soldiers each time who happened to be in front of a given house. This was -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Do you have -- you have yourself discussed the matter with inhabitants, with the citizens of this town?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally discussed the matter with the locals and with the soldiers. I asked them whether they'd had a good rest, whether there were any problems. There was no sign of friction, no sign of discontent. It all seemed perfectly normal. An hour later we completed our visit and we drove back to Jablanica believing that there was no cause for concern, that everything was all right. There were no problems whatsoever. At least, there hadn't been up to that point. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Right. Now, you're speaking about this as if it had been a necessity for the troops to be billeted in this city, in this town, that there was no other solution or possibility. Was that true? Was it the case?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: If we had known, if we had been able to assume that this would happen, we would never have allowed it. Even if the soldiers had to sleep rough. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] No. First of all, did this happen before the incident? Did it happen that the troops would be billeted with civilians of another ethnic group, or was it the very first time that this happened?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: There were Croats in Jablanica, Croats who lived there at the time in and around Jablanica. Specifically, the inhabitants of Grabovica were consulted. They behaved in a natural way and thought it was all right to put the soldiers up. We, as an inspection team, faced an insurmountable difficulty, given the number of refugees in the area, Jablanica being absolutely overcrowded with refugees flooding in from the surrounding areas where Muslims had previously been expelled from their homes. So they all converged in Jablanica, which as a result was heavily overcrowded. Had it not been for this situation, we certainly would not have remained adamant that these soldiers should be accommodated in Grabovica. We simply lacked logistics to do anything else. We had no tents, no equipment, nothing we could use for these soldiers to set up camp. On the other hand, they needed rest after a long and strenuous march and we couldn't just let them sleep rough with no roof over their heads. And this is what led us to decide to find accommodation for them in Grabovica. But one thing is certain: We never expected that what eventually happened would ever happen. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] This is my last question. It has to do with -- do you remember when you made your decision to billet the troops in Grabovica, was this decision forwarded by whatever means to the chief of the inspection team? Was he informed?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Knowing that the units from Sarajevo would arrive and knowing their numbers, which was about 200 men, having got in touch with the Municipal Staff in Jablanica, having been aware of the situation there, that Jablanica was overcrowded and that accommodation was short, several days prior to their arrival we concluded that we should go to Grabovica. We concluded that we should try and find a solution together with the local inhabitants, to ask them to put the soldiers up for one or two nights so they could get a rest before the operation commenced. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And the chief of this inspection team, was he made aware of this decision? Was he told?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honours, Honourable Chamber, I can't say that he was informed specifically about this one decision, because the person we are talking about, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, Sefer Halilovic, was outside Jablanica at the time. He wasn't present. But it was very much in keeping with the overall idea, and as a team we had to deal with it. We believed we were not doing anything that was not allowed. This was part of our competencies, that we were a team meant to coordinate combat operations and deal with certain problems. I'm not sure I'm making myself perfectly clear, am I? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] No. The question is to know whether according to the military structure a leader of a team is normally put on notice of any decision which is made within the team. Isn't it the case?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: That is certainly the case. However, this is a minor detail which after the incident was transformed into something really important, after the crime had occurred. But as we were still preparing the operation, there was no way we could know what would happen to the people in Grabovica and we had no time to go round and try to track down the chief, who was elsewhere going about his own business. This was a routine matter for this to be set up. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's happened. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are there any questions by the parties at this stage? Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Just a few questions. Examined by Ms. Chana:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karic. I'm Sureta Chana. I'm counsel for the Prosecution. I'll ask you a few questions, if I may. In -- in response to Their Honours' question --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to you in respect of billeting of the soldiers, did Sefer Halilovic ever tell you not to billet the soldiers with civilians?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: We didn't discuss this matter in detail at the time. We tried to carry out our tasks in keeping with the general idea and with the order that had already been written. We believed that it was a routine matter that we had to deal with. When I say "we," I mean the inspection team. We didn't think it necessary to go back to the chief for every single thing, for every little thing, because he was elsewhere. He was not in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But what about before the soldiers went to Herzegovina and the meeting that you alluded to when His Honour Judge Liu asked you that you had a meeting before about the billeting of the soldiers with Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours -- sorry. Perhaps -- I'll let my friend finish the question before I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was discussed at this meeting when it did come to billeting of soldiers? Because it's an obvious question which would have been raised. Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps before the witness answers, I object to that. Your Honours, the leave granted by this Chamber is very confined to specific matters. That's what we're all prepared for here. This question offends in two ways: First of all, the witness has given general evidence concerning this matter; but secondly, it doesn't concern paragraph 10 of the indictment. Your Honours have given us a very precise range for our questions. I'll be bound by it too, of course. But my learned friend is. And to go to the content of meetings on previous occasions seems to me and in my submission is plainly outside of the leave that you have granted. So I object to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I also have some problem with this question, that is, about that meeting. It's not specific enough. You know, which meeting you refer to in this situation. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in response to your question, you said -- he said there was a meeting where these things were discussed, and I was just trying to clarify. And perhaps I could ask the witness: Was there such a meeting? Because he did say that before there had -- this had been discussed. This -- this is in response to your question. Your Honour, I'm merely asking questions which arise out of Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you some leeway in this aspect and to see how far we could go.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, was this ever discussed, the question of billeting soldiers when they would reach Herzegovina, at any meetings prior to the soldiers leaving from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I understand your question. There were a number of practical matters that we had to deal with. One of them, as I've mentioned, was the matter of finding accommodation for the units, of creating propitious conditions in Jablanica for the troops to rest. We, as the inspection team, were every day at the forward command post. This is what we used to call it at the time, and this was at the hydro power plant in Jablanica. There was a building there. And before we arrived, the Municipal Staff used to be in that building. They gave us two offices to use so that we could go about our daily tasks. It was in those offices that we were in touch on a daily basis. We knew that there were units arriving from Sarajevo and we made the decision. If Sefer was there or if he was not there several days previously is not something that I can say, but we believed this to be a perfectly natural decision at the time. That was what we believed before the crime happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, Mr. Karic, the question is really quite simple. Was this discussed, the billeting of the soldiers, prior to their billeting with Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's two objection. That wasn't the question. If you look and see what was asked before, it wasn't that. And secondly, my friend is not to cross-examine. Now, Your Honours granted some leeway, but I'd submit this has now gone far enough. An answer has been gained to the question. It's clear what the sense of that answer is. Now, I'd submit that's enough and I object to this question on specific and general grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana, you could ask a question for the clarification concerning this witness's testimony of that meeting, but not a kind of umbrella question trying to seek some evidence before the billeting of the soldiers in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll put it this way, Mr. Karic: Did Sefer Halilovic ever ask you where the soldiers were to be billeted when they reached Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I want to -- that question. If the witness could just excuse me. This question has got an assumption built into it which is not legitimate given the evidence of the witness. The question asks -- the question presumes that Sefer Halilovic knew that these troops were going to Grabovica. If you see there the specific word "Grabovica" is used. Now, the evidence of this witness is quite clear about that, and this question is illegitimate because it's got a presumption built in that's not only one that the witness hasn't agreed to but it's one that the witness has positively said is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But, however, the witness has already answered that question. We'll adjust, you know, these questions and answers, taking into consideration of your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As I said, he has already answered that question. You'll find it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in response to Judge Liu's question, you -- you said there was -- soldiers had been billeting in Gornja Jablanica with civilians prior to these soldiers being billeted in Grabovica. Was Sefer Halilovic aware of this billeting in Gornja Jablanica, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes, to the extent that he would have had to know, being the head of the team. We had to find accommodation somewhere, and I told you about the area being overcrowded, about Jablanica being overcrowded, and I've explained why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there civilians in Gornja Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: There were civilians residing there, refugees too, locals. Wherever we could, we used the area to find accommodation for elements of the 10th Brigade, Caco and Topalovic's -- Caco Topalovic's brigade in the Gornja Jablanica area. This was perfectly natural to have people rest for a night or two so they didn't have to sleep rough, and there was no problem with that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your evidence, Mr. Karic, that you were not ordered by Sefer Halilovic in any way, manner, or form to billet these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, again that's cross-examining. Again, it's been answered on numerous occasions. And this is not permissible, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that this question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will -- I will now take you to another subject, Mr. Karic. You said you went to Grabovica on one day before and one day after. Now, can I ask you: When you went to Grabovica after the soldiers had already been billeted there, where is it that you went, location-wise?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, the composition of the group was what it was, and I told you also who drove us to Grabovica, where the previous day we had consulted the Croat inhabitants and had obtained their approval to have the soldiers billeted there. We visited all the houses, starting with the ones next to the railway station and those just across the bridge near the Grabovica hydro plant, and the last houses were the last houses in the village, several hundred metres down the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have a meeting with the soldiers as a group, or was it just individual -- going to individual houses?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the soldiers were never lined up. We believed that this was perfectly natural. We were a group. We were a inspection team. We went around together. We inspected houses and we visited all the groups of soldiers who had spent the night there and who were in the yards in front of the houses. We also talked to those locals who had offered their hospitality. We talked to both, and neither seemed to have any problem at all. Everybody seemed happy, the soldiers and the local residents alike. An hour later, roughly speaking, we visited the last house and the last group of soldiers that were still around, after which we drove off to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, I want to be quite clear about this. Are you saying you just -- you visited groups of soldiers, or was it one meeting with a -- with a group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is a second try, I would say a third try, at the same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think the witness answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We -- here we just want to know -- I believe the Prosecution wants to know whether there's a get-together of the soldiers, whether the witness addressed the soldiers or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, look, if it assists the Trial Chamber, I won't object to it, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, did you address the soldiers as a group, one big group?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: There was no particular address. This was a normal, human, soldierly talk. We greeted the groups that were in front of the houses that had stayed there, that had spent the night there, that were resting, sitting outside. It was nice weather. I recall that it was sunny. And we went like this from house to house, from group to group. But there was no gathering of soldiers or any kind of meeting, or there was no particular address to the group. We had -- I had people from the inspection team together with me, Zicro Suljevic, Rifat Bilajac, Namik Dzankovic. We didn't separate. We walked together shoulder to shoulder from group to group, from house to house. We didn't encounter any problems that would intrigue us so that we would go into any kind of meeting that would call for resolution of any kind of problem. There were no questions either. Everything was normal. Everyone was satisfied, one side and the other. And I am repeating this. Who knows how many times over can you not believe honourable people who spent their whole lives in an honourable way who were with me shoulder to shoulder, than some asocial types who provided statements that I said that if there were any problems, you can kill them and throw them into the Neretva River. Two or three asocial drugged persons are believed who [as interpreted] committed those crimes and not people who went with me, who are honourable generals of this army and have for their whole working lives lived honourably as men. This is something that I am surprised at, that I wonder about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not make any such utterances as you have just alluded to in your answer, that people who do not give hospitality, you can kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, again, I object. Firstly, he's made that absolutely clear. Absolutely clear. Secondly, it's cross-examination, once again. And so I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think this issue is very clear --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- Ms. Chana. Maybe you could ask a question to make sure Mr. Halilovic was not with the group.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe Judge El Mahdi asked that question, but I will certainly ask it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, was Sefer Halilovic present at this time that you were going from this group to group of soldiers in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: No, Sefer was not present. He was not in Jablanica on that day. He was in the northern part of Herzegovina, somewhere in Konjic, Buturovic Polje. In any case, he was outside of Jablanica, outside Grabovica. I said which people were with me on the two occasions, without Sefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That will be all from me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Morrissey, do you have any questions to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The Prosecution's covered the legitimate areas I can ask questions about. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, I understand that there are some documents used in the deposition procedures and they have not been admitted into the evidence. Are there any documents to tender at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- some of the documents which were used in the deposition have already been tendered, except for the diary and the transcript of the -- of the witness. The others are already exhibits, Your Honour, and we are not seeking to tender the diary and the transcript of -- has already been tendered, of the deposition. I think that's already been agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So at this stage there are no documents to tender.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you could give me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: While the Prosecutor is doing that, Your Honour, could I just mention that in your order you requested the registrar to assign an exhibit number to the transcript of this document, which I believe has been done already. But it may have to be formally done in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for the deposition will be 444.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other was the transcript of his OTP interview that was alluded to in the deposition, and we would now seek to -- that's the only document which is not in evidence, which is MFI P1 -- sorry, MFI P2, the transcript of the interview given to the OTP, and we would seek to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But as a general rule, if we have the opportunity to have this witness in life, the previous statement will not be admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a special situation. If you look back at that deposition, there was -- there was a time when this witness made many statements which were in conflict with his prior statement. And rather than impeach him at that time to save time and rather than use him as an adverse witness, they introduced his earlier statement, and it was a matter to save time and it was also a matter related to this witness's health, which we all know that there is a problem related to his health, without getting into that matter. And as a result, that statement should be admissible, either that or the -- this should be allowed to -- this hearing should remain open and let's use him as an adverse witness. Which would be foolish because of the health considerations, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any comments on that, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'll restrain the comments to those concerning the use of the document, and I'll leave for a later time and I will raise at a later time when it's not in such a hurry the impropriety of the submission that has been made and the way in which it was made. At the moment, this document was not put to the witness at the time. It's not relevant. The witness has given evidence in a deposition and here. Furthermore, Your Honours made a ruling on this question in terms of how matters were to proceed here. The Defence made submissions about the use of these documents and -- in those. And in my submission, it's implicit in -- in that ruling that you will see his -- watch the deposition and -- and -- and then have limited questions here. The using of these interviews, attended as they were with all sorts of considerations, is a dangerous thing to do at any time. It's particularly dangerous and offensive to try to do it with a witness who was not put as an adverse witness, but, on the contrary, who was called by the Prosecutors to prove part of their case and was led and put before the indicting Judge. There are a large number of objections to this. If it's not sufficient to deal with it now on the basis of which I've -- I've heard, then I would seek to be able to put all this into a motion. But the short answer is probably the one that Your Honour raised: There's nothing special about this situation at all. The Prosecutor had every possibility to put that to Mr. Karic at the time, chose not to. The conduct of that deposition was absolutely disgraceful in all respects by the Prosecution, which I'll amplify if needs be. And they shouldn't now be permitted to get this document into evidence at the last gasp, as they now try. So I submit you can deal with it quite easily at this point. But if Your Honours are in any doubt about it, then we'd seek leave to file a motion about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one brief comment.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: This was -- this issue was in fact raised at the deposition at page 76. And the presiding officer at that time said that it would be a matter for the Trial Chamber. That's on page 76. So this was sent to this Trial Chamber from the presiding officer at the time of the deposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It seems to me that we are not in the position at this stage to make a ruling concerning with this document. If there are any supplementary comments or information for the tendering of this document and for the objection of the tendering of this document, the parties will file a motion to this Trial Chamber by next Monday. It is so decided. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for giving your testimony. The Bench --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The Bench wishes you a speedy recovery and to take good care of yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So the hearing is over. We'll take a break. And we will resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that we could have some time to deal with some housekeeping matters, especially with the admission of the documents. The first matter I would like to say is about the proposal made by the Prosecution for the tendering of the interview with the accused in 2001. And at this stage the Trial Chamber is considering whether to admit it or not, taking into the account the objections filed by the Defence. This Bench requests the Prosecution to indicate the parts of the interview which are relevant to the present case which they seek to have admitted into the evidence, since we found that this interview is extremely long and some parts are not entirely relevant to the present case. And also to the extent possible, to indicate which paragraphs of the indictment those parts are in support of. The Prosecution shall submit the above-mentioned information by Thursday, 9th of June. The next issue will come to the specific documents tendered from both sides. The first document is MFI 221, a document submitted by the Defence. That is a report by Namik Dzankovic sent to the military. I would like to know about any objections to the admission of this document by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very quickly, I believe that document is already in evidence, that it was just mistakenly placed on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just confirm that that's correct. Your Honours, we think MFI 215 and MFI 2 -- MFI 215 and MFI 221 are the same document, and since they are the same document, the Defence would not continue to press for 221 to be admitted. Now, Your Honours, that's subject to one small reservation, which we can deal with later, if necessary. I'll just flag it now. We don't have to do anything about it. If it turns out that the translation of the two is different, then we'll refer the matter back to CLSS to decide on any -- on any difference. I don't believe there are material differences. And if we find a difference, we'll seek to reopen the matter. Meanwhile, we're happy, since they're the same document, not to push ahead with asking 221 to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. So the next issue is the document 256 and 264, both documents tendered by the Defence. And I see no objections from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So these two documents are admitted into the evidence. The next issue is about 375, tendered by the Defence. And we would like to hear from the Prosecution about their view on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a document that concerns propaganda. It was published by the HVO for Bosnian troops, as the Court recalls. Kate Adie is the witness that was shown the document. She had never seen it. She was not aware of it. And she did not follow or implement it. There was no evidence as to its authenticity. There's no evidence as to who received it, whether it was ever sent out or whether it was ever implemented. There's no evidence that it was intercepted by the other side, the ABiH army, that it was sent up to their line, that the accused saw it, or that anyone in the command saw it. There's no evidence that it was followed. Therefore, there's a question as to its authenticity. There's a question as to its relevance and materiality. It was not implemented or it was not used in this case, and it has no relevancy to this case. As a result, we oppose the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's not one of our better ones, Your Honour. We say it's relevant because of the way that the crime scene was -- unfolded and we say that it's chain -- the chain of custody is that it came from the Croatian State Archive, so that it would not normally be a document that could be proved through any of these witnesses. But the matters that my friend has pointed to are all relevant ones for you to consider. Frankly, here in the end Ms. Adie did not adopt that document, nor did she find it of particular significance to herself. So in these circumstances we offered it for tender at the time, but I have to say that the Prosecution -- what the Prosecutor said are entirely relevant matters for you to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So this document is not admitted into the evidence. The next three documents are documents 390, 415 we mentioned before, I believe, as well as 419. Those documents were tendered by the Prosecution, so I would like to seek the views from Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be clear, we are dealing now with two transcripts, one with -- between the accused and Vahid Karavelic, and the other between the accused and Ramiz Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I'm told that 415 is -- is different. That's -- that's one of the MUP reports. I apologise for that. Could I just indicate about the transcripts, that the Defence has -- we've spoken to the Prosecutors and we're taking the view that we're not opposing each other's transcripts effectively, that we don't argue against that. Therefore, I withdraw any reservations which I previously put on the record -- well, perhaps I'll put it another way. I had indicated I wanted to reserve my position about the Karavelic and -- and Ramiz Delalic transcripts. Can I indicate that we do not oppose those being tendered into evidence because the Defence are seeking to tender documents as well of exactly the same sort and provenance. As to 415 -- can I just confirm that's one that Your Honours are now concerned with, 415?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that is a MUP report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honours, we -- we maintain our objection to 415. That, again, falls into the category of MUP reports upon which the Defence find themselves embarrassed because we don't know who made it, when, whether the information is reliable. It's never been suggested for one second that Halilovic saw this MUP report. And as with most of those MUP reports, the Prosecutor didn't try to establish that Sefer Halilovic saw that document. So that we oppose it -- we continue our opposition to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you want to -- to make a reply?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This MUP report is no different than other MUP reports which have been entered into evidence, Your Honour. This particular MUP report was shown to Delalic in respect of the information contained therein, which was about the criminality of the 9th Motorised Brigade. And there is no difference between this MUP report which -- and a lot of the others which were admitted through Jasarevic, who said this is operative information. Your Honours of course will look at the weight such documents will carry, and that is up to Your Honours' discretion. But for admissibility, Your Honour, I feel it's -- the Prosecution submits it's relevant and probative and it should be admitted as -- as a MUP report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Bench believes that this document has some relevance to our case, and also it has some probative value for this document, so we decided that it is admitted into the evidence, as well as the document 390 and 419. So those three documents are admitted into the evidence. The next batch of documents is the document 424, 425, and 428. The document was tendered by Mr. Morrissey through the witness Delalic. I understand there are some objections from the Prosecution. At this stage, are there any things to add from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Could I just indicate this: That this morning, not knowing how Your Honour wanted to proceed, we filed a motion concerning these documents. I can put the argument orally here. We don't require that -- and I'll put exactly what's in the motion. It's short. It's short. The issue with those letters was that they were -- the Defence wished to lead them in evidence as a spontaneous reaction by those in Sarajevo. The fact is documents like that are usually not admitted, and in these circumstances, if the Prosecutor was prepared to consent to them being admitted from -- I mean, they're documents from the bar table, Your Honour. That's the reality about them. If the Prosecutor consents to them being tendered, then they can be tendered. If the Prosecutor maintains their position, that unfortunately for us is the end of the question at this stage. So if the Prosecutor consents, I'm happy; and if not, I think Your Honours have no -- no option but to -- to refuse to admit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The Prosecution maintains its objection to these three documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Therefore, these three documents are not admitted into the evidence. But I have to say that this decision is without prejudice to the future introduction by the parties if - if - we find it relevant to our case through future witnesses in the Defence case. It is so decided. The next documents are two documents, that is, documents 431 and 434. Those two documents are tendered by the Prosecution through the witness Bakir Alispahic. Mr. Morrissey, are you in the position to -- to say your position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour -- sorry, would Your Honour just give me one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's best to deal with these now, if possible. If you'd just give me one moment, Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We object to both, Your Honours. The first one is -- the first one is 431. That's the document concerning the alleged massacre at Klis, K-l-i-s. Now, this was a poisonous document. The Prosecutors in that -- the information in that document is that Halilovic ordered Ramiz Delalic to go and massacre and rape and burn a particular village. The Prosecutors did not put that document to Ramiz Delalic, didn't ask him about it. Instead it comes to Mr. Alispahic. He considered it. He said it was unreliable. Now, it's just a piece, in the Defence's submission, of poisonous gossip that is so far from anything to do with the case and so far from reality that the -- that the Chamber should simply dismiss it as being too remote to be of any assistance to you. It's not a document that could ever have been shown to Halilovic. Now, the Prosecution may from time to time show documents which are supposed to have put Sefer Halilovic on notice. So if there was a report about Caco and the 10th Brigade or Celo and the 9th Brigade which was shown to Halilovic. Of course that's relevant for the Prosecution to lead, even if they can't prove where it comes from or what weight it had. And such evidence, I believe, was led or at least a small portion of such evidence was led. But this document could never have been shown to Halilovic. It involves Halilovic. It says Halilovic is the author of the killings. No one suggests it was shown to him, and common sense reveals that it couldn't have been. Therefore, as well as being poisonous and prejudicial, it's just irrelevant to these proceedings. There's a further issue that it lies way outside of the proceedings. Your Honours, we would be here until 2009 if we had to deal with every allegation made by Ramiz Delalic against Sefer Halilovic. Murdering the commander in chief is one. But this one didn't come through Ramiz Delalic. It's just a document that we shouldn't have to deal with and we'd ask that Your Honours cut this unwelcome guest out of the trial at this stage. As to the next -- and perhaps I should say this, too, Your Honours: That my learned friend Ms. Chana would confirm this, that although in court here Mr. Delalic wasn't confronted with that document, my learned friend Ms. Chana can indicate to you whether or not he was confronted with it, as Ms. Chana would, as a matter of fairness, have been obliged to do and I'm sure she will confirm that she did confront Mr. Delalic with it during that interview. And of course, you know, has you can imagine -- I won't say what's in it. The Prosecutor can tell you. But I mean, this -- anyway, I've said what I've had to say about that, Your Honour. And I'll become verbose as I already have on the topic. The next one, 434, we object to that for a different reason. That is the document signed by Mr. Mujezinovic, a witness who the Prosecution withdrew after having moved this Court strongly at a late stage to include. Now, Mr. Mujezinovic is said to be the author of this document, although he's not here to prove that he was. But it's a document dated in -- in October. It's after Grabovica. And it's concerned with Halilovic's own allegedly bad behaviour. It's not relevant. The Prosecution is not allowed to throw mud at Halilovic and to cast aspersions on his character. They may lead evidence before the crimes that he was on notice or, if they had any such evidence, they might be allowed to lead evidence after the crimes that he covered up the crime or that he failed to do something that -- that the Prosecution says he should have done. But to lead evidence that he was vain, self- promoting, and wanted the media to cover him well, is irrelevant, and it's prejudicial. And by "prejudicial" I don't mean harmful to him. There's a lot of prejudicial material in trials that hurts the accused. That's not prejudicial. That's just evidence. This is prejudicial because it creates a bad atmosphere about Halilovic which is irrelevant and which is hard to find. Because it means that we have to go back and call evidence about -- well, from -- I suppose from newspaper editors or -- I don't know where you turn, frankly. But we shouldn't have to meet that. It's just outside of what the Prosecution is entitled to prove, and it has -- it has a prejudicial effect with no probative value. That's relevant not just to weight. It's relevant to whether you add it to the trial record here and put us in a position where we have to decide do we extend the trial fighting these sort of allegations or do we not. So in my submission, you can leave that one out on that basis. There is a further reason, of course: that Mr. Mujezinovic could have been brought here and wasn't. Now, the Prosecutor is entitled to make a decision about Mujezinovic. The Chamber has already indicated the rules you'll apply when the Prosecutor makes the decision. Frankly, the Prosecutor has to run its own case. We well, understand that. But when you take Mr. Mujezinovic out, you can't, then, put in his documents, unless by consent. And with this one here, we do not consent. Those are my submissions about those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any reply from the Prosecution? Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, briefly, on 431, the first one. We clearly aren't relying upon an allegation in there in relation to Mr. Halilovic's personal participation in the alleged events in Klis, and Mr. Alispahic made it quite clear he couldn't comment on that. It's not quite correct, as my learned colleague said, that -- Defence colleague said that it was -- had no reliability. Mr. Alispahic's evidence was it was at the lower end of reliability because it was a first -- it was a first source which had to be corroborated by any others. But the -- the parts about this -- about this particular document we rely upon are to show that soldiers from Sarajevo had been there before and had been brought back and had been brought back because of bad behaviour, and that was something that was known to those who should have known. Mr. Alispahic, the Minister of the Interior, knew about it. And if he knew about it, it is so unlikely that the army command, Mr. Halilovic as the Chief of Staff, would not have known about it, that it would be almost virtually impossible for them not to know about these troops being brought back for bad behaviour. Now, Mr. Alispahic's evidence was that some of it, some of the information, was true but he wasn't going to go into any specifics. So it's just a -- a document that is broadly corroborative of other evidence about the reputation of those particular brigades. We put it -- we put it no further than that. So that's that one. The second one is 434. That, in our submission, is in the same category as the other MUP reports. Mr. Morrissey again raises the issue of Mr. Mujezinovic. Well, had we known before today that the Defence was not objecting to the intercepts going into evidence, Mr. Mujezinovic would not have been on our witness list. So that -- the Mujezinovic issue, in our submission, is entirely a red herring. But what this document goes to show is basically the view of Mr. Halilovic -- which is held by those who were investigating his conduct at the time, which is corroborated by the evidence already led in this case. Mr. Hodzic was his own journalist, who almost -- it would appear on the evidence Mr. Halilovic's personal journalist who was following him or covering -- covering large aspects of Mr. Halilovic's own activities. We've heard evidence the Defence introduced it about pictures of Mr. Halilovic being on a police station. There's been evidence of Sefer Halilovic badges. So all this goes towards the mens rea or the motivation of Mr. Halilovic in bringing the soldiers from Sarajevo to assist in his own -- to assist his own desire to rehabilitate himself in the eyes of the -- the Bosnian Presidency and the command, and there's evidence of that in numerous documents. There are a number of document which is have been tendered, as to the view of the security services as to what Mr. Halilovic was doing. So it's another broadly corroborative document which goes to Mr. Halilovic's mens rea at the time. But I mean, these two documents aren't, I add, make-or-break documents for the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after consultation with Judge El Mahdi, I came to the conclusion that the document 431 is not admitted into the evidence since we believe that the evidence in that document is far remoted from the case we are hearing now, and we are not quite sure whether this document could assist us or not. utterances.text: Counsel began by saying that there is no tendering documents from the bench. Every week in this Tribunal documents are tendered from the bench or from the bar table, every week. In that case hundreds - we're not talking about one or two - hundreds of documents were tendered from the bar table. And at one point during that case the Prosecutor moved to tender approximately 1.000 documents, which were a total of 3.000 pages, from the bar table, of which a number of them were objected to, and that's why these decisions had to come. And in that case, at page 22 it states - and I'm just reading paragraph 15, the first few sentences: "The first question arises is whether the admission of a document without its purported author or another individual who can testify to the document being called as a witness constitutes in itself a violation of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. As already stated by the Chamber in its previous section of this decision, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal is clear on this matter. There is no principle of blanket prohibition on such documents." We will respond in writing to any of their claims; however, I -- I think it should be clear on the record the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is that documents may be tendered from the bar table. Thank you.

utterances.text: I need to respond to that. If Mr. Re has a witness that will indicate that all of those things he has said are true, he may ask you for leave to call that witness.
