utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. You may proceed, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just with respect to that chart, I should say the Defence would -- would want to be heard about that in the future because a chart produced by the Prosecutor's military experts the Defence will no doubt say is wrong. And -- and would -- would want to cross-examine somebody upon it if such a chart was to be produced. But, however, there may be a simpler way to do it than to go to the military expert. There is, in fact, in evidence a chart that was put there Mr. Karavelic. That chart is a little difficult to read. And you may recall that both the Prosecutor and myself had some difficulty in focussing on the broken lines as opposed to the hard lines there. Now, that chart might be amenable of graphic improvement so that it can be done in a way that all of us can understand without changing the meaning or adding any Prosecution or indeed Defence hopes. Your Honours, there's -- just one little stroke of a pen can change everything. So we -- you know, what we would like is that -- is that perhaps that could be the basis. And we couldn't object to that. If it's a military expertise from the Prosecutors, we would object to it, Your Honours. But perhaps I can speak to my friend about that and we'll see if we can reach some common ground. If we can't, we'll come back to you. Your Honours, the next issue I wanted to raise was concerning the EDS, electronic discovery suite, and the disclosure that occurs on it. Now, it's occurred in recent cases not this one but the Limaj case and other cases that there have been some controversy of the operating of this system. It has got some real problems with it. And those problems are not to be raised by the Defence when a nasty document suddenly jumps up at the last minute, because at that time the witness is already there; the Chamber is obviously aware that the document exists, and there's a temptation to use it and to want to see it. And therefore the Defence really want there to be some clear rules of engagement and rules by which we proceed in the using of such material. Now, what has happened in some previous cases and what happened in the Limaj case quite recently is that at a very late stage when a witness came to give evidence material prejudicial to that witness was disclosed to the Defence, very late. It was said at the time by the Prosecutors - and the Defence is not entering into a good-faith analysis about all this - that it just happened that they found it at that late time. But the EDS system, Your Honour, is just very difficult to use from the Defence point of view. We find ourselves constantly unable to find documents on it. I don't know and I don't presume that Your Honour has a great in-depth knowledge of how that system works, but my understand is as follows: The EDS system is a storage facility onto which data that the Prosecution has in its possession is placed. It has two categories that are able to be searched: There's a general category; and then there's a case-specific category. There are various ways in which that -- that database can be searched by both the Prosecutors and the Defence, and on that database is to be found -- are to be found many documents. The Prosecution have said in other cases, and it may be their position here, that they discharge discovery obligation by placing on the EDS material that comes into their possession. And one can see from the Prosecutor's point of view that they handle many documents and that they -- although they are well resourced, they might not be well enough resourced to hand deliver every document to the Defence, and we accept that there's some need for facility of that nature to exist. But the difficulty is that it's very hard to search - and the Defence experience is that it's hard to search. The Prosecutors say, as I don't know whether they will in this case - I suspect they will - that they don't have any problems to search and they can search. But our experience is that it is a absolutely nightmare. As a test you can have that document in front of you. You can try and find that document that you know exists, that you have the ERN numbers for, and you can't find it. In other occasions, you can do find it. So it's an unpredictable tool and it's very difficult. But further, the Defence simply does not have the resources to constantly check this -- this electronic discovery suite. We cannot do it. I can say it no plainer than this. The breakdown of the hours that we work is already relatively outrageous. We work hard. The staff I have work very hard. They cannot do that. We do not have the resources to look at it. We are not going to look at it. We can't. We can't do our job and do that. And therefore what is needed is for the Prosecutor to indicate to us -- they don't have to provide us with paper copies of the documents but they have to give it an indication when they are updating that system in a way that concern it is Halilovic case. All we need from the Prosecutors is an indication, "Today we placed these document numbers," and a short description of those documents, "on the EDS. They need to tell us what's gone on there, because we can't check, and we know -- we suspect that there's -- we have a suspicion that by shaking tree, thing wills fall down. We think there be material. We think that a lot has gone on now that we've reached this stage. What we want -- and we're going to move a motion to the effect -- we've written to the Prosecutors. And we're going to move a motion to the effect that unless the Prosecutors agree to what we put in the letter, we'll move the Tribunal to make some rules about this. You don't have to give the Defence everything they want but we need some rules to indicate what's going on, because otherwise we will not be in a position to know what the Prosecution has put on the EDS. We cannot monitor it like policemen, so we need to be told what's going on. And it's very important that we say it now so that the Prosecution has time to respond rather than to say it as a time later when we look like we're hiding behind a fig leaf because we're embarrassed about a particular witness being shown his -- a film of him committing crimes or whatever it be that that happens. And so we need to know these things in advance. And we don't want to be put in the position of troubling the Tribunal with people who shouldn't be called, people who are -- you know, about whom there's dreadful material. So I indicate that, that we are going to move a short motion concerning the EDS and the rules to be applied, unless the Prosecutors and I can come to an agreement over this -- this topic. I flag it now. They can say what they want here, of course. I've mentioned it so they can respond. But I'm not asking you to rule but I have to put it on record now at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Very brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Defence filed a letter to us. The letter will be -- a response to their letter on this matter will be filed today. Mr. Sachdeva has been working on it and indicated it will be completed before the day's over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I see. What's the contents of that? Is there any agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I haven't seen the letter. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may it please you. There are some issues in the letter that we will not agree with in terms of obligations, disclosure obligations under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's the theoretical issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Exactly. But in terms of informing the Defence when collections are placed on the EDS, as I understand it that is an OTP-wide issue that is being dealt with at the moment. And at this stage the Prosecution will obviously endeavour to inform the Defence when we have placed collections on their specific disclosure suite index. That will be done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hope that after this sitting both parties could meet on this issue and try to prevent any filings from the Defence, because we have been troubled, you know, with all those motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll -- we will meet with the Prosecutors and we'll try to resolve our differences in a way that doesn't involve the Tribunal in further work. And we acknowledge that there has been a number of filings. We have to say that if you don't file, then we inflict upon the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm not depriving your right to file anything. I mean that before any filings, the parties should meet together, try to solve it, you know, off the court. If there's, you know, a major problem that you could not solve, we are ready to give the assistance to the both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that indication. And next of all, there are some -- some outstanding requests and letters that we have with the Prosecution. I'm grateful to my learned friend Mr. Weiner who responded to me last night concerning some aspects of the 1996 Halilovic statement which is the subject of a motion. But there are still a couple of matters that are of importance, and the ones I want to raise here concern the witness Ramiz Delalic, that there are statements that plainly exist and plainly are out there somewhere and they still haven't been provided to the Defence, and we don't know what's happening with those now, so we need -- we need some sort of answer to that -- that query. So what's outstanding is -- is, if you like, notes of the investigators and -- and the statements themselves. I should hasten to say that we have been provided with some material and we're grateful for the effort that has so far been made, but on the face of things it's quite clear there still are outstanding materials, and so that we need the Prosecutor to tell us what the progress is on those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. In respect of Mr. Delalic's -- what is referred to as "previous statements," the -- the Defence had noted through some investigation and reading of the transcripts of this -- of the statements that somewhere it's stated that there was a 1996 statement. Now, I have already spoken to the Defence about this at length. I have taken the trouble, Your Honours, to ring up the two previous investigators to see if there was any written statement which emerged from the discussions. I have not come to any conclusion because it appears that there isn't one. And I've given the details to the Defence in respect of that, and I'm willing to put it also in a -- in a letter so that -- So for us -- for them to now say that there is a previous statement, there simply -- we do not have one in our databanks. I think we can confirm that always subject to a caveat that gets thrown up to us. But there simply -- whatever has been disclosed in respect to Delalic. Your Honours, I also looked into the -- any notes of the investigators, and to that end, although there was a Rule 70 internal documentation of mission reports which the investigators made after they came back, I even disclosed some of those to the Defence, some of the notes that they had taken. So I have in all good faith, Your Honour, made my investigations into this. Of course, I cannot say that they've been absolute. There never is such a thing. But whatever I could find, even to the extent of what I said, lifting Rule 70 and disclosing to the defence some of the notes. It's not a happy situation for the Defence, and I do appreciate that. But as of now we do not have any other statements given to the OTP. If there were contacts made between Delalic and investigators here, we have no further records of it that we can hand over to the Defence. That is the position of the Prosecution with respect of this. Your Honours have a lot of the -- of matters to deal with, and to -- and I think it would be important to put an end to certain issues. And I would like to sort of say that perhaps this might be the time to end this particular issue of Delalic. Wherever it falls, that's where it's fallen. And the Defence will simply have to accept it to the extent that these are the inquiries and these are the fruits of the inquiries which have been hand over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that there is not much things to fall after shaking the trees on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence draws a distinction between the individual Prosecutors and the Prosecution as an institution. We are very grateful for the efforts made by Ms. Chana, and we accept fully that they were made in good faith. What she has put to you about providing us with working notes in an attempt to assist us is entirely accurate, and certainly we are not suggesting that Ms. Chana is behind anything strange that might have happened to this statement. The fact remains we have statements that were taken. There's clear evidence that statements exist, that somewhere they're out there. There's evidence from Mr. Delalic himself that he made a statement to the -- to the OTP. The question of where it is remains a live one because the -- there seems to be two possibilities arising out of it that: Perhaps Mr. Delalic was just lying and there was no such statement; or perhaps a subsequent investigator at some stage has interposed himself into the picture. No other explanation appears to -- possible at this point. The Prosecution's good-faith inquiries raise troubling questions. That's the reality. But, Your Honours, all that my friend can do is make the inquiries that she makes, and I acknowledge that there's a certain point at which she can only look once or twice or three times at a particular set of documents. We do not ask you to order her to do more. The Prosecution have clarified the position in court as best they can. It's not the end of the matter. Ramiz Delalic is not going to go away in this trial, I can assure everyone of that. But in any event, my learned friend can't be compelled to do more than what she has now subjectively done. I think she's right to say she has done all she can. We'll -- we're going to make further inquiries of the Prosecutor, however; there's no question about that. However, that seems to put an end to that matter from the Chamber's point of view for today. The next matter concerns the provision of material to be used by the Prosecutors in cross-examination to the Defence. Now, the Prosecutors are in a different position to the Defence at all times. This Chamber made a decision on the 9th of May, 2005 at which it was said, "The disclosure of material and information by the Prosecution is fundamental to the fairness of the proceedings before the Tribunal. The Trial Chamber therefore endorse it is view that in order to avoid a possible prejudice to the accused, which might result from the Prosecution introducing documents in the cross-examination of a witness which the Defence had never had the opportunity to review, the Prosecutor must bona fide disclose to the accused -" and I'm leaving a passage out there - "to the accused at the earliest available opportunity and at the latest prior to cross-examination any new material it wishes to submit to a Defence witness in cross-examination in order to give the accused due notice." Now, that is another aspect of the same matter I raised with the EDS. Experience shows that it simply isn't enough to place these things on the EDS. These things have got to be explicitly disclosed. If they are on the EDS, we will be satisfied with a short note and an ERN number. These matters in any event ought to be raised with the Prosecutor. As I've indicated, I'm going to discuss with them these matters later. We may need to come back to the Tribunal about that at a future time, but it's to be avoided if we can. So I raise it now. I indicate it's an issue, but we may be able to resolve that. If we can't, however, Your Honour may need or the Tribunal may need to put time limits on that ruling of yours, whether you're going to say 48 hours before, 24 hours before, or some other figure. You may be called upon to adjudicate that if we can't agree with the Prosecutors as to a suitable time limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe we'll have the 65 ter Conference as well as the Defence conference in the future. That might be a good time if you want to bring to our attention on this matter after consultations with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And of course, it -- it of course has to be noted the Prosecutors can't really do much until they know who we're calling, and we acknowledge that that's a burden for them. So there's nothing they can do today. Finally, the issue of Rule 68 obligations has to be faced in exactly the same context. Now, it's always said it's an ongoing obligation, which it is, of course. But we are now at the end of the Prosecution case, and it's high time that the Prosecutors indicated in a thorough way what the situation is. Should material arise concerning, for example - and I use this just as an example - Ramiz Delalic, then the Defence is placed in a position where we haven't used that in cross-examination, and the sooner we have it, the better. So that we ask the Prosecutors to -- to make a special effort now, rather than have things arise throughout the trial, throughout the presentation of the Defence case. History shows that in some trials the Defence case is provided with a great deal of relevant material to Prosecution witnesses too late during the Defence case. That -- of course it's an ongoing obligation. Sometimes the Prosecutors do find something at a late stage. What we're asking now is that they look very hard now so that belated material does not arise. And in particular I would ask that the Prosecutors indicate now -- so that they are satisfied that they have performed a thorough search and that there is no more Rule 68 material in their possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly in response to that. The Prosecution continually does update its searches of all materials in-house, so whenever something that arises that is Rule 68 or Rule 66(B), we will, of course, disclose that to the Defence. This is common policy within the OTP. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. I believe this matter is also a subject matter for the parties to discuss. Now we have seen that this issue is flagged in the transcript. So if there's any problem in this aspect, the Bench is ready to help both parties to solve this issue. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that terminates the list of matters that I had to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As Mr -- yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have one issue of a document that was never given an exhibit number. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's MFI 162. Our case manager had just alerted this to us. It wasn't on the list that the court deputy provided to us a few days ago. It's simply a photograph that was shown to a witness Katica Miletic on the 9th of February by the videolink. You may recall we put this on the -- the ELMO and tried to show her, and it didn't actually get an exhibit number. It's at page 20 to 21 of the transcript. So we just seek an exhibit number for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that it is already admitted into the evidence. Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I -- I can't recall that specific one. I haven't reviewed that transcript. If the document was shown to the witness and if she -- and if she was asked questions about, I -- might I just trouble the Prosecutor to provide me with a hard copy of it? I could just look at it to see if there's any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- anything ... Your Honours, I think this is one of the documents that was -- one of two documents, that this was shown and then another one was marked and each was tendered. I don't have any objection to this. I believe -- I think it's in evidence too, Your Honour. But if it hasn't been given a number, I don't -- I don't take it that the Prosecution are tendering it now. They're just seeking that it be given a number, and I don't oppose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just checked the database, and I see that 162 is a photo. Can I see the photo. But it has not been admitted. So just to -- to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll make a decision that this document is admitted into the evidence, and the -- and the number will be assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the number is 162, so it's just a matter of admitting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Well, as the Defence counsel said, we are now at the end of the Prosecution's case and as the practice of other Trial Chambers, at this stage or around the time for the 68 bis filings of the Defence, the Prosecution is requested to submit a proofing chart. In this proofing chart, they have to indicate the evidence as to each paragraph in the indictment. Now, since the Defence counsel give up their right to activate their 98 bis procedures, in the view of this Bench the Prosecution still have to file a proofing chart to summarise their case. So at this stage, I hope that the Prosecution could file it before the 13th of June, which might be helpful for the Defence to prepare their case. It is so decided. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'm grateful for that indication. And might I just say that one thing that would speed up the trial, I imagine greatly, is that if the Prosecutors are able in that proofing chart to indicate where a document is relevant to a particular -- I imagine that's probably part of it anyway, but it's the Defence plan in this case - and I think that's been obvious from the start - to put as many documents and as much of our case as we can through the Prosecution case. And we will double up our documents with the Prosecution to a significant extent. And if the Prosecution are able -- the more specific the Prosecution are about the documents they use and the relevance of those documents, the more focussed we will be able to be about the documents that we put in. But as I indicate, we've put in a lot of documents here. The Prosecution have been very patient in many ways with us in that -- that endeavour. But we will save time if that's done. So I mention that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that's the usual practice in the submission of this proofing chart. Yes. I think that's all for today's hearing, and the hearing is adjourned.
